notes_list.title: Hyperconjugation (Baker-Nathan Effect)
notes_list.basic_overview: Hyperconjugation (also known as the Baker-Nathan effect or no-bond resonance) involves the delocalization of σ electrons from a C–H or C–C bond adjacent to an electron-deficient center (empty p orbital of a carbocation or radical) or a π system (alkene or arene). This orbital interaction stabilizes carbocations, free radicals, and substituted alkenes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The orbital overlap involved is primarily σ(C–H) → p (in carbocations/radicals) or σ(C–H) → π* (in alkenes). Reverse hyperconjugation (isovalent hyperconjugation) occurs in halo-substituted compounds like -CF3 groups where lone pair density donates back into σ*(C–F) antibonding orbitals.
notes_list.examples: 1. Carbocation stability: (CH3)3C+ (9 α-H) > (CH3)2CH+ (6 α-H) > CH3CH2+ (3 α-H) > CH3+ (0 α-H). 2. Alkene thermodynamic stability: Tetrasubstituted > Trisubstituted > Disubstituted > Monosubstituted. 3. Carbon-carbon bond length shrinkage: C(sp3)-C(sp2) single bond in propene is shorter (1.50 Å) than in propane (1.54 Å).
notes_list.conditions_and_medium: Requires proper stereoelectronic alignment: the σ(C–H) or σ(C–C) bond must lie in the same plane as the vacant p orbital or π* orbital (coplanar/parallel orbital geometry). Rigidity preventing coplanarity disables hyperconjugation.
notes_list.mechanism_steps: 1. Locate α-carbons directly attached to the electron-deficient center (sp2 C+ or sp2 C=C). 2. Count the number of α-hydrogens bonded to these sp3 α-carbons. 3. Align the α C–H σ orbital parallel with the unhybridized empty p orbital or π* antibonding orbital. 4. Draw canonical hyperconjugative forms showing partial double bond character between C(α)–C(sp2) and proton release (no-bond resonance forms).
notes_list.kinetics_and_energy: Each α-hydrogen contributes ~1.5 to 2.0 kcal/mol of stabilization energy to a carbocation. In alkenes, heat of hydrogenation (ΔH_hyd) decreases with increased alkyl substitution due to hyperconjugative thermodynamic stabilization.
notes_list.selectivity_and_stereochemistry: Determines Saytzeff vs. Hofmann elimination selectivity (Saytzeff product with more α-H is more stable), controls regioselectivity in electrophilic addition reactions (Markovnikov's rule via carbocation stability), and governs ortho/para orientation of alkyl groups in electrophilic aromatic substitution.
notes_list.common_traps: 1. Counting β or γ hydrogens (ONLY α-hydrogens attached to sp3 carbons directly adjacent to the sp2 center participate). 2. Assuming C–D bonds offer identical hyperconjugation: C–H hyperconjugates better than C–D due to higher ground-state zero-point vibrational energy (Kinetic Isotope Effect). 3. Calling it actual bond breaking—no-bond resonance is merely a canonical representation of orbital delocalization.

exam_focus.level: IIT-JAM / MSc entrance / GATE concept depth
must_revise: α-hydrogen count determination in cations, radicals, and alkenes
σ(C–H) → p vs σ(C–H) → π* orbital interactions
Heat of Hydrogenation (ΔH_hyd) comparison in isomeric alkenes
Secondary Kinetic Isotope Effect (C–H vs C–D hyperconjugation)
Reverse hyperconjugation in trichloromethyl / trifluoromethyl benzenes
